headline: Trump expands AI data center pledge to governors and utilities, aiming to lower electricity costs
summary: President Trump has expanded his "ratepayer protection pledge" to include 23 state governors and 187 utility companies, aiming to control spiraling electricity costs driven by AI data centers. Critics question its legal enforceability.
details: President Donald Trump has expanded his "ratepayer protection pledge," now signed by 23 state governors and 187 utility companies and data center developers. This initiative aims to curb rising electricity costs, largely driven by the massive power demands of AI data centers. Signatories include major utilities like NextEra Energy and data center giants such as Equinix.

The pledge, first introduced in February, was intended to make electricity more affordable for American families. Energy Secretary Christ Wright previously stated it would deliver "more affordable, reliable, and secure energy." Trump reiterated promises that electricity bills would come down.

Despite these assurances, the initial promise has shown little effect on electricity rates. PJM Interconnection, the largest power grid operator, recently billed Maryland $2 billion for grid upgrades to support out-of-state AI data centers. An independent watchdog linked a 75.5% increase in power costs in the region directly to data centers.

The administration is pushing for accelerated AI adoption to maintain global supremacy, believing states must support data center development. However, public pushback is growing due to concerns over electricity costs, water quality, and noise pollution. Several jurisdictions, including Seattle and New York, have implemented temporary bans on new data center developments.

Critics argue the pledge is merely a promise without legal enforcement. California is reportedly attempting to pass legislation to codify these promises into law. Oregon has already enacted the POWER Act, forcing large electricity consumers (over 20 megawatts) to pay their true costs, leading to a 30% increase for data centers and a 1.3% cut for residential users.
